nodes.label: REST endpoint scaffold
nodes.one_line: Generate a REST endpoint — route, handler, response — with AI assistance and get it responding correctly to a real request.
know_what: REST endpoint — a route bound to an HTTP method (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE) with a handler and a defined response shape, the smallest deployable backend unit
Request/response contract — the shape of what an endpoint accepts and returns, which must be pinned down before or during scaffolding so client and server agree
Status codes — using 200/201/400/404/500 correctly instead of always returning 200 with an error message in the body, a common AI-generated shortcut
Route framework conventions — the specific patterns of Express, Fastify, or Hono (middleware order, handler signature) that an AI must follow rather than invent
curl / HTTP client verification — testing an endpoint directly with a real request tool, independent of any frontend that might also be broken
Idempotency — whether calling an endpoint twice with the same input produces the same result, relevant for GET and PUT but not for POST by default
know_how: Define the request and response shape before or alongside the first scaffold prompt
Test the endpoint directly with curl or an HTTP client, not only through a frontend that could mask the real response
Check that the endpoint returns the correct status code for success, client error, and server error cases
Confirm the endpoint follows the framework's actual middleware and routing conventions, not a generic pattern the AI defaulted to
Verify the endpoint against malformed or missing input, not just a well-formed example request
habits: Hit every new endpoint with curl or an equivalent tool before considering it done
Check the response status code explicitly, not just that a response body came back
Test with an empty or malformed request body as a matter of course
Read the handler's error path, not just its success path, before accepting the scaffold
Confirm the endpoint is registered on the router the way the rest of the codebase does it
nodes.checkpoint: Given a spec for a single endpoint (method, path, request shape, response shape), scaffold it and verify with curl that it returns correct status codes for a valid request, an invalid request, and a missing resource.
nodes.common_failure: Scaffolding an endpoint that only handles the exact request shape shown in the prompt's example, returning a raw 500 or an unhandled exception for anything else — verified only by a demo request, never by an edge case.

nodes.label: Schema design
nodes.one_line: Design a database schema, by hand or with AI assistance, well enough to defend every table and relationship in it.
know_what: Schema — the set of tables, columns, types, and relationships that define what a database can store, the artifact a whole backend is built on top of
Normalization — structuring data to avoid duplication and update anomalies, and the specific tradeoffs (join cost, query complexity) of normalizing further
Foreign key — a column constrained to reference another table's primary key, which an AI will sometimes omit in favor of an unconstrained id column that looks the same until data goes wrong
Nullable vs required column — deciding whether a field can be absent, a decision with real downstream consequences for every query and every piece of code that reads it
Index — a structure that speeds up lookups on a column at the cost of write performance and storage, needed for any column queried or joined on frequently
Migration-friendliness — designing a schema so future changes (adding a column, splitting a table) are additive rather than requiring a risky rewrite
know_how: Draw out every table and its relationships before generating any migration or ORM code
Decide and state explicitly which columns are nullable and why, rather than accepting an AI's default
Add foreign key constraints for every relationship, not just an unconstrained id column that happens to hold the right values
Identify which columns need an index based on expected query patterns before the schema is finalized
Walk through the schema's ability to answer the app's actual known queries before accepting it as done
habits: Sketch the schema by hand or with a diagram before letting an AI generate migration code from it
Ask 'what breaks if this column is null' for every column before marking it nullable
Check that every relationship has an actual foreign key constraint, not just a same-looking id column
Walk through the app's known query patterns against the schema before considering it final
Treat a schema change to a shipped table as a bigger decision than a schema change to an unshipped one
nodes.checkpoint: Given a feature description (e.g. 'users can comment on posts'), design a schema with correctly typed columns, foreign keys, and nullability, and defend every nullable column and every foreign key's ON DELETE behavior.
nodes.common_failure: Accepting an AI-generated schema where every relationship is just a plain integer or string column with no foreign key constraint — it works until inconsistent data creeps in, at which point nothing in the database itself was ever enforcing the relationship.

nodes.label: ORM wiring
nodes.one_line: Have an assistant wire an ORM or query layer to the schema and verify the generated queries actually match the intended relationships.
know_what: ORM — a library (Prisma, Drizzle, TypeORM, SQLAlchemy) that maps database rows to application objects and generates queries from a schema definition
N+1 query — a pattern where fetching a list plus a related field per item issues one query per item instead of one join, a common AI-generated ORM mistake
Eager vs lazy loading — fetching related data up front in the same query versus fetching it on demand later, and the performance and correctness consequences of picking wrong
Generated SQL inspection — reading the actual SQL an ORM call produces, since the ORM's method name doesn't guarantee the query does what it implies
Schema-ORM drift — the ORM's model definitions falling out of sync with the actual database schema, a source of confusing runtime errors
know_how: Log or inspect the actual SQL generated by an ORM call during development, not just trust the method name
Check any query returning a list-plus-relation for an N+1 pattern before considering it done
Confirm the ORM's schema/model definitions match the real database schema after any migration
Test an ORM query against a realistic data volume, not just one or two rows, since N+1 patterns are invisible at tiny scale
Choose eager or lazy loading deliberately per query based on what's actually needed, not by ORM default alone
habits: Check generated SQL for any query touching more than one table
Run a new ORM-backed endpoint against a seeded dataset with realistic row counts, not just one row
Re-sync ORM model definitions immediately after every schema migration
Treat an ORM call in a loop as a red flag worth reading closely
Confirm a relationship's ORM-level cascade behavior actually matches the schema's foreign key ON DELETE setting
nodes.checkpoint: Given an endpoint that returns a list of items with a related field for each, identify whether the ORM call produces an N+1 query pattern by inspecting the generated SQL, and fix it if so.
nodes.common_failure: Trusting an ORM method name (like .include() or .with()) to mean the data is fetched efficiently — some patterns compile to a single join, others silently issue one query per row, and the only way to know is to look at the generated SQL.

nodes.label: Auth flow
nodes.one_line: Implement a real authentication flow — sessions or tokens — with AI assistance, understanding every step well enough to spot a missing check.
know_what: Session-based auth — a server-stored session referenced by a cookie, versus token-based auth (JWT) that's self-contained and verified without a server-side lookup
Password hashing — storing a salted hash (bcrypt, argon2) rather than plaintext or a fast general-purpose hash, non-negotiable regardless of how the rest of auth is built
Authorization vs authentication — confirming who a user is (authentication) versus confirming what they're allowed to do (authorization), two separate checks an AI can conflate or skip one of
Token expiry and refresh — a short-lived access token paired with a longer-lived refresh token, and the specific flow for renewing one without forcing a re-login
Auth library vs roll-your-own — using a maintained library (Auth.js, Passport, Lucia) versus implementing sessions or JWTs by hand, a real tradeoff in control versus battle-tested correctness

Common auth vulnerabilities — session fixation, missing CSRF protection, JWTs verified without checking their signature or expiry, all patterns an AI can reproduce from training data as easily as the correct version
know_how: Verify passwords are hashed with a slow, salted algorithm (bcrypt/argon2), never a fast hash or plaintext
Check every protected route enforces authorization, not just that a login endpoint exists
Test the full flow by hand: register, log in, access a protected route, let a token expire, log out
Confirm JWTs (if used) are verified for signature and expiry on every protected request, not just decoded
Choose a maintained auth library for anything beyond a toy project, and understand exactly what it's doing under the hood before trusting it
habits: Walk the entire auth flow by hand — including the expiry and logout paths — before calling it done
Check every new protected route for an authorization check, not just assume one earlier check covers it
Verify password hashing algorithm and salt explicitly rather than trusting it looked right in the diff
Treat any custom auth code with extra scrutiny compared to a maintained library's code
Re-test the auth flow after any unrelated change that touches routing or middleware order

know_why.claim: Auth should be built on a maintained library rather than implemented by hand, even though an AI can generate a plausible hand-rolled version.
know_why.because: Auth vulnerabilities (session fixation, token verification bypass, timing attacks on comparison) are subtle and well-studied; a maintained library has had many more eyes and real incidents shape its defaults than a single AI-generated implementation has had review.
know_why.disputed_by: Some practitioners in the agentic-autonomy and vibe-loop schools argue a small, fully-understood hand-rolled auth flow is safer for a small project than a large, partially-understood library with its own surface area of misconfiguration risk.
know_why.source: OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet; practitioner debate on build-vs-buy for auth

nodes.checkpoint: Given a basic app, implement a full auth flow (register, login, protected route, logout, token expiry) with hashed passwords and enforced authorization on every protected route, verified by hand end to end.
nodes.common_failure: Implementing a login endpoint and a protected route separately, each individually working, without verifying that the protected route actually rejects an unauthenticated or unauthorized request — the gap between the two pieces is exactly where an AI-generated auth flow tends to have its real hole.

nodes.label: Input validation
nodes.one_line: Add server-side validation and sanitization to AI-generated endpoints so the client is never trusted with the last word.
know_what: Server-side validation — checking input on the backend regardless of what the frontend already checked, since the backend is the actual trust boundary
Schema validation library — a library (Zod, Yup, Joi, Pydantic) that validates and types incoming data against a declared shape, catching malformed input before it reaches business logic
Sanitization vs validation — rejecting bad input (validation) versus cleaning it into a safe form (sanitization), two different operations often conflated
Injection risk — unsanitized input reaching a database query or shell command, the specific class of bug input validation exists to prevent at the boundary
Client-trust assumption — the specific, dangerous default an AI can fall into when a frontend already validates a field and the backend skips re-checking it
know_how: Validate every field of every incoming request on the server, regardless of frontend validation
Use a schema validation library rather than ad hoc if-checks scattered through handler code
Test an endpoint with malformed, missing, and unexpected-type input, not just valid input
Confirm rejected input returns a clear 400-class error rather than causing a 500 or, worse, being silently accepted
Check that validation happens before any database query or side effect, not after
habits: Never trust that a frontend's validation makes backend validation optional
Send malformed requests directly to an endpoint (bypassing the frontend) as a standing test habit
Read a new endpoint's validation schema against the full set of fields it accepts, checking nothing was missed
Flag any endpoint that reaches a database call before validating its input
Confirm error messages from failed validation don't leak internal details unnecessarily
nodes.checkpoint: Given an endpoint that accepts user input, send it malformed and missing-field requests directly (bypassing the frontend) and confirm every one is rejected with a clear error, none reaching the database.
nodes.common_failure: Relying on frontend form validation as the only check, because the endpoint 'always' receives requests from the app's own frontend during testing — anyone hitting the endpoint directly (a script, a modified request, another client) bypasses it entirely.

nodes.label: Migration discipline
nodes.one_line: Generate and review database migrations with AI, checking that each one is reversible and doesn't silently drop data.
know_what: Migration — a versioned, ordered script that changes a database schema, the mechanism that keeps a schema's history reproducible across environments
Reversible migration — a migration with a working down/rollback step, versus a one-way migration that can only be undone by hand or from a backup
Destructive migration — one that drops a column, table, or data outright, which needs a higher bar of review than an additive one
Migration ordering — running migrations in the same sequence across every environment, since running them out of order can leave a database in a state no migration file describes
Backward-compatible migration — a schema change deployed before the code that depends on it, so a brief window with old code and new schema (or vice versa) doesn't break
know_how: Write and test a migration's rollback step before running the migration on any real data
Review any migration that drops a column or table with extra scrutiny, confirming the data loss is actually intended
Run a new migration against a copy of realistic data before running it against production
Sequence a schema change to be backward-compatible when code and schema can't deploy in the exact same instant
Confirm migrations run in the same order in every environment, not just locally
habits: Treat every destructive migration as requiring a second, deliberate confirmation before running it
Test a migration's down/rollback step, not just its up step
Run new migrations against realistic data volumes before trusting them on production
Keep migrations small and additive where possible, splitting a risky one into safer steps
Check migration order matches across every environment before assuming they're equivalent

know_why.claim: A migration should be reversible before it's ever run against real data.
know_why.because: An AI-generated migration that looks correct can still be wrong in a way that's only visible once it's run against real data shapes; without a tested rollback, the only recovery path left is a backup restore, which is slower and lossier than a rollback.
know_why.disputed_by: Some practitioners argue writing and testing a rollback for every migration is disproportionate overhead for a young project with no production data yet, and prefer to add rollback discipline only once real user data exists.
know_why.source: Database migration practice literature (Rails/Django migration conventions; practitioner discussion on migration safety)

nodes.checkpoint: Given a migration that adds a required column to an existing table with data, write it as a backward-compatible, reversible migration and demonstrate the rollback restores the prior schema cleanly.
nodes.common_failure: Running a migration that looks correct in isolation without testing it against a copy of real data — a required-column migration that works on an empty test database can fail outright, or silently corrupt existing rows, once real data with unexpected shapes hits it.

nodes.label: Error-handling contract
nodes.one_line: Define and enforce a consistent error-response contract across AI-generated endpoints instead of an ad hoc shape per route.
know_what: Error-response contract — a fixed shape (e.g. { error: { code, message } }) that every endpoint's error response follows, so clients can handle errors generically
Error code taxonomy — a stable set of named error codes distinct from HTTP status codes, letting a client distinguish 'email already taken' from 'invalid email format' even though both are 400s
Internal vs external error detail — what's safe to expose to a client (a validation message) versus what should be logged internally only (a stack trace, a database error string)
Uncaught exception handling — a global error handler that guarantees any unhandled exception still returns the contract's shape instead of a raw framework error page
Contract drift — individual endpoints each inventing their own ad hoc error shape over time, which an explicit contract and its enforcement are meant to prevent
know_how: Define the error-response shape once, in one place, before endpoints are written rather than after they've each invented their own
Route every thrown error through a single global handler that enforces the contract shape
Check that internal details (stack traces, raw database errors) never reach the client response
Assign a stable error code to each distinct failure case, not just a generic message
Test an endpoint's error responses directly, not just its success response
habits: Check every new endpoint's error responses against the shared contract, not just its success response
Trigger an unhandled exception deliberately to confirm the global handler still returns the contract shape
Scan error responses for leaked internal detail (stack traces, raw SQL errors) before shipping
Flag any endpoint that returns an error shape different from the rest of the API
Keep the error code list in one place so it doesn't quietly diverge per endpoint
nodes.checkpoint: Given three endpoints each written in a separate session, verify all three return errors in the exact same shape, including for an uncaught exception, and fix any that drift from the contract.
nodes.common_failure: Letting each AI session invent its own error response shape for the endpoint it happened to be working on — early on the differences look cosmetic, but they compound into a frontend that needs special-case handling per endpoint instead of one generic error handler.
sources: JSON:API error object spec (as a reference shape)

nodes.label: Background jobs
nodes.one_line: Move slow or scheduled work into background jobs or queues with AI assistance, verifying failure and retry behavior by hand.
know_what: Background job — work moved off the request/response cycle (sending an email, processing an upload) so a slow operation doesn't block the client waiting on it
Job queue — a system (BullMQ, a Sidekiq-equivalent, a managed queue) that holds pending jobs and hands them to workers, distinct from just calling a function asynchronously in-process
Retry policy — how many times and with what backoff a failed job is retried before being treated as permanently failed, which an AI's first draft often omits entirely
Idempotent job design — writing a job so running it twice (from a retry) doesn't double-charge, double-send, or otherwise duplicate its effect
Dead-letter handling — where a job that's exhausted its retries ends up, so a permanently failing job is visible and investigable rather than silently vanishing
know_how: Move any operation slower than a couple hundred milliseconds, or any operation with an external dependency, out of the request/response cycle into a job
Design each job to be safely re-run (idempotent) before wiring up retries
Set an explicit retry count and backoff policy rather than accepting a queue library's silent default
Test a job's failure path deliberately (make it throw) to confirm retries and dead-lettering behave as expected
Monitor the job queue's failure and backlog counts, not just whether jobs were enqueued
habits: Ask 'what happens if this job runs twice' before shipping any new job type
Deliberately fail a new job once in testing to watch the retry and dead-letter path actually fire
Check queue depth and failure counts periodically instead of assuming enqueued jobs always complete
Treat a job with no defined retry policy as unfinished, not just conservative
Review any job touching money or user-facing communication with extra care for idempotency before shipping
nodes.checkpoint: Given a job that sends a confirmation email, design it to be idempotent, set an explicit retry policy, and demonstrate that a deliberate failure retries correctly and lands in a visible dead-letter state after exhausting retries.
nodes.common_failure: Shipping a background job with no retry policy and no idempotency guarantee — the first transient failure (a flaky network call) either silently drops the job forever or, once a naive retry is added later, duplicates its effect (a second email, a double charge) because the job wasn't designed to be safely re-run.
